11523.content:
DatasetGenerator is a DataAdapter that samples points from several multivariate Gaussian components. It receives component means, covariance matrices, desired record counts, and a random seed, then fills a standard numeric Dataset.

The seed makes generated experiments reproducible, while labels identify the generating component for later cross-tabulation. Using the same adapter interface as a file reader lets algorithms ignore whether records were loaded or simulated.

11526.title: Gaussian Kernel Classifier
11526.heading: Gaussian Kernel Classifier
11526.content:
A Gaussian kernel classifier assigns high similarity to observations separated by a small squared Euclidean distance and lets similarity decay exponentially with distance. The corresponding implicit feature space supports flexible nonlinear boundaries.

Kernel width determines locality: a narrow kernel can form intricate regions around examples, while a broad kernel behaves more smoothly. Feature scaling is essential because the kernel converts raw distances directly into influence.

11529.title: Gaussian Covariance Regularization
11529.heading: Gaussian Covariance Regularization
11529.content:
Gaussian covariance regularization adds a nonnegative epsilon term to covariance estimates before inversion or likelihood evaluation. It prevents a component concentrated on too few or collinear points from producing a singular matrix.

The parameter trades numerical stability against fidelity to the unregularized maximum-likelihood estimate. It should be reported because changing epsilon can alter responsibilities, convergence, and the selected clustering.

11532.sourceSearchName: gauss s law gauss s law
11532.title: Gauss's Law
11532.heading: Gauss's Law
11532.content:
Gauss's law states that the electric flux through a closed surface is

$$\oint E\cdot dA=\frac{Q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}.$$

Only enclosed charge contributes to the net flux. With sufficient symmetry, the law converts a surface integral into a direct calculation of electric field strength for spherical, cylindrical, or planar charge distributions.

11535.title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination
11535.heading: Gauss-Jordan Elimination
11535.content:
Gauss-Jordan elimination continues row reduction above as well as below each pivot until the coefficient matrix reaches [[Reduced Row Echelon Form]].

The method can expose a solution directly without [[Back Substitution]]. Applying the same operations to $[A\mid I]$ reduces the left block to $I$ and produces a [[Matrix Inverse]] in the right block when $A$ is nonsingular.

11537.heading: Document

11538.sourceSearchName: gauss seidel method gauss seidel method
11538.title: Gauss-Seidel Method
11538.heading: Gauss-Seidel Method
11538.content:
The Gauss-Seidel method updates the components of an approximate solution sequentially. Each new component is used immediately when computing the remaining components in the same iteration.

This often converges faster than the [[Jacobi Method]], though convergence is still not automatic. It is the special case $\omega=1$ of [[Successive Over-Relaxation]].

11541.heading: Gaussian Cluster Covariance
11541.content:
Gaussian cluster covariance describes the spread, orientation, and correlations of one mixture component. In several dimensions, constant-density surfaces are ellipsoids determined by the covariance matrix.

Constraining covariance matrices across components defines different model families, from equal spherical groups to clusters with distinct volumes, shapes, and orientations.

11544.content: A gas-turbine plant compresses air, burns fuel to heat it, then expands the hot working gas through a turbine that drives both a compressor and an electrical generator. The source presents natural gas or oil as fuels. Exhaust leaving the turbine still carries substantial heat, so a [[Combined-Cycle Power Plant]] can use it to raise steam instead of simply discharging it.

11547.title: Garbage Collection
11547.heading: Garbage Collection
11547.content:
Garbage collection reclaims managed objects that are no longer reachable. Frequent temporary allocations increase the amount of memory the collector must examine and can add work to a heavily used request path.

The book compares custom request parsing with ASP.NET Core model binding to reduce unnecessary object creation. Allocation changes should be measured under load because simpler code and lower allocation may matter more than hand-written parsing assumptions.

11550.title: Garbage Mattes for Key Extraction
11550.heading: Garbage Mattes for Key Extraction
11550.content: A garbage matte quickly removes portions of a shot that lie well outside the subject before a fine key is attempted. It need not follow every hair or moving contour; it only reduces the area where the keyer must distinguish the subject from its screen. A narrow band of screen can remain near the subject for the key to resolve. In the book's crowd-shadow example, a roto garbage matte first isolates the performer before the blue-screen key is pulled. This coarse-to-fine division saves detailed keying work.

11553.title: Gap-Constrained Sequence Pattern
11553.heading: Gap-Constrained Sequence Pattern
11553.content:
A gap-constrained sequence pattern allows matched elements to be separated while limiting the permitted gap lengths. It captures ordered relationships that need not be contiguous but should remain locally related.

Tighter gap bounds reduce accidental matches and search complexity; looser bounds provide invariance to intervening events. The appropriate constraint follows from the sequence's domain and scale.

11556.title: Gamma Distribution
11556.heading: Gamma Distribution
11556.content:
The gamma distribution is a continuous probability family restricted to positive values. Its shape and rate parameters can represent varying degrees of right skew and tail weight, making it suitable for quantities that cannot be negative.

The source introduces it while modeling gene-specific variability, whose distribution is positive and heavy-tailed rather than normal. The chi-squared and exponential distributions arise as special cases under particular parameter choices.

11559.title: Gamma Camera
11559.heading: Gamma Camera
11559.content: A gamma camera maps photons emitted by a [[Radioactive Tracer]]. A collimator accepts selected directions, a scintillation crystal converts gamma energy to light, and photomultipliers estimate event position and energy. Accumulating accepted events forms an image of tracer distribution and therefore physiological function rather than only anatomy.

11561.sourceSearchName: games as a service games as a service
11561.title: Games as a Service
11561.heading: Document

11562.sourceSearchName: games as a service games as a service
11562.title: Games as a Service
11562.heading: Games as a Service
11562.content:
Games as a service treats deployment as the beginning of an ongoing product cycle. The team repeatedly plans, develops, deploys, supports, measures, and learns from changes used by a live player population.

This operating model connects product development with service reliability. Release speed has value only when the game can be observed, supported, and changed safely after deployment.

11563.sourceSearchName: games as a service games as a service
11563.title: Games as a Service
11563.heading: References

11565.title: Gamer Dedication
11565.heading: Gamer Dedication
11565.content:
Gamer dedication is a scale describing how much time, knowledge, money, attention, and effort a person invests in games and game culture. It replaces a rigid core-versus-casual binary with several observable dimensions.

Dedication affects tolerance for complexity, learning, long sessions, and specialized equipment, but it does not determine genre taste by itself. A target audience should be described with the dimensions relevant to the proposed game.

11568.title: Gameplay
11568.heading: Gameplay
11568.content:
Gameplay is the set of challenges a game presents and the actions it permits the player to take, both to overcome those challenges and to perform other enjoyable activities. It is the active relationship between player and rules.

A setting, story, or visual style does not specify gameplay by itself. Designers must state what the player repeatedly does, what resists those actions, and how the system responds.

11571.title: Gameplay Stress
11571.heading: Gameplay Stress
11571.content:
Gameplay stress is the time pressure placed on a player while attempting a challenge. It increases difficulty by reducing the opportunity to plan, check work, or recover from an error.

Stress is distinct from intrinsic skill. Changing a timer, enemy pace, or response window can alter stress without changing the underlying action the player must perform.

11573.title: Gameplay Scripting
11573.heading: Document
11573.content:
2026-09-18 17:13

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Scripting and Data Formats]]

11574.title: Gameplay Scripting
11574.heading: Gameplay Scripting
11574.content:
Gameplay scripting implements frequently changed rules, events, quests, interfaces, or object behavior in a higher-level language connected to the game engine. Scripts usually trade some execution performance for faster iteration and easier authoring.

The engine exposes selected functions and data rather than unrestricted internals. This boundary keeps performance-critical systems in native code while allowing game-specific behavior to change without rebuilding the entire engine.

11576.title: Gameplay Mode
11576.heading: Document
11576.content:
2026-09-18 16:43

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Design Process and Roles]]

11577.title: Gameplay Mode
11577.heading: Gameplay Mode
11577.content:
A gameplay mode is a coherent configuration of available gameplay, camera model, and interaction model at a particular time. A significant change in any of those elements means the player has entered another mode.

Modes limit complexity by offering an appropriate subset of actions and information. Their transitions must be understandable because the player needs to know what can be done, how the world is viewed, and how control now works.

11580.title: Gameplay Engine
11580.heading: Gameplay Engine
11580.content:
A gameplay engine is a systemic loop that reinforces or balances the same kind of [[Resource]]. It differs from a [[Game Economy]], which gains value by exchanging resources, and a [[Game Ecology]], which balances through exchange.

Engines can add capability through a [[Boosting Engine]] or regulate it through a [[Braking Engine]]. These structures often sit inside larger mechanics and progression systems rather than appearing alone.

11583.title: Gameplay Animation
11583.heading: Gameplay Animation
11583.content:
Gameplay animation uses motion to communicate the state, character, and relationships of game objects. Speed, rhythm, direction, and posture can make an object appear aggressive, cautious, vulnerable, or important.

Animation also acknowledges input and state changes. A pushing motion can confirm that movement input was received even when a wall blocks progress, while blinking or color flashing can indicate temporary invulnerability or a successful hit.

11585.title: Game
11585.heading: Document
11585.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Mechanics and Rules]] · [[Game Definition and Forms]]

11586.title: Game
11586.heading: Game
11586.content:
A game is a voluntary activity organized within a distinct rule-bound context, with goals, meaningful choices or conflict, and a recognizable outcome. Individual examples may not exhibit every trait equally, so games are better treated as a family of related forms than as a rigid checklist.

A functioning game is not only rules or content. It is a [[Game-Player System]] in which a player acts on a dynamic [[Game Model]], receives [[Feedback]], and builds a [[Player Mental Model]] through play.

The source identifies four essential elements: [[Play]], [[Pretending]], at least one arbitrary and nontrivial [[Game Goal]], and [[Game Rule|rules]]. These elements distinguish a game from an unstructured toy, a purely practical task, or a passive presentation.

11588.sourceSearchName: game player system game player system
11588.title: Game-Player System
11588.heading: Document

11589.sourceSearchName: game player system game player system
11589.title: Game-Player System
11589.heading: Game-Player System
11589.content:
The game-player system treats the game and the player as interacting subsystems of one functional whole. The game supplies a dynamic model and feedback; the player supplies intentions, decisions, actions, and learning.

Neither subsystem alone creates the played experience. Their reciprocal exchange forms [[Interactivity]], produces [[Engagement]], and supplies the higher-level whole observed and changed through the [[Designer Loop]].

This exchange can be understood as a [[Game as Conversation|conversation]]. The creator speaks through rules and context, the player responds through verbs and choices, and the system's resistance and feedback shape what each action means.

11590.title: Game-Player System
11590.heading: References

11591.title: Game World
11591.heading: Document
11591.content:

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game World and Expressive Play]]

11592.title: Game World
11592.heading: Game World
11592.content:
A game world is the artificial universe in which game events occur. It can be a simulated space containing characters and objects or a more abstract setting established through rules and representation.

The world gives context to actions and goals, but not every game needs an elaborate fictional place. Its dimensions should support gameplay rather than accumulate detail that the player cannot use or perceive.

11594.sourceSearchName: game world realism game world realism
11594.title: Game World Realism
11594.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game World and Expressive Play]]

11595.sourceSearchName: game world realism game world realism
11595.title: Game World Realism
11595.heading: Game World Realism
11595.content:
Game world realism is a continuous, multivariate relationship between a designed world and familiar reality. Graphics, physics, scale, behavior, causality, social rules, and consequences can each be more abstract or representational.

Realism should be selected separately for each aspect according to player expectations and gameplay needs. A simulation may simplify controls for accessibility, while a stylized game may preserve realistic consequences where they make choices meaningful.

11596.title: Game World Realism

11598.sourceSearchName: game world object registry game world object registry
11598.title: Game World Object Registry
11598.heading: Game World Object Registry
11598.content:
A game world object registry stores the objects that participate in particular phases of the [[Game Loop]]. Separate collections can track [[Updateable Game Object|updateable]] and [[Drawable Game Object|drawable]] objects so each phase iterates only applicable instances.

Creation adds an object to the required collections, and removal must take it out of them. Centralizing this membership gives the loop a consistent view of the active world while preserving different object capabilities.

11599.sourceSearchName: game world object registry game world object registry
11599.title: Game World Object Registry
11599.heading: References

11601.title: Game Verb
11601.heading: Game Verb
11601.content:
A game verb is a [[Game Rule]] that gives the player liberty to act within the game. It is a rule through which the player can change the system, such as moving, jumping, firing, rotating, or placing a piece.

Verbs are the player's side of the [[Game-Player System|game-player dialogue]]. They let the player test other rules, learn how [[Game Part|game objects]] behave, and make [[Meaningful Decision|meaningful decisions]]. A focused set of verbs gives a design a clearer interactive vocabulary.

11603.sourceSearchName: game ui screen resolution game ui screen resolution
11603.title: Game UI Screen Resolution
11603.heading: Document

11604.sourceSearchName: game ui screen resolution game ui screen resolution
11604.title: Game UI Screen Resolution
11604.heading: Game UI Screen Resolution
11604.content:
Game UI screen resolution is the pixel dimension within which interface elements are rendered. A layout authored for one resolution can become too small, stretched, or misplaced when displayed at another size or aspect ratio.

Resolution-aware UI uses anchors, reference dimensions, and [[Game UI Coordinate Conversion]] to preserve hierarchy and usable target sizes. Text and detailed artwork may require separate assets or scaling policies rather than uniform enlargement.

11605.sourceSearchName: game ui screen resolution game ui screen resolution
11605.title: Game UI Screen Resolution
11605.heading: References

11606.sourceSearchName: game ui middleware game ui middleware
11606.title: Game UI Middleware
11606.heading: Document

11607.sourceSearchName: game ui middleware game ui middleware
11607.title: Game UI Middleware
11607.heading: Game UI Middleware
11607.content:
Game UI middleware supplies an external authoring and runtime system for building interface layouts, animation, and behavior. Artists and content creators can iterate in a visual tool while programmers integrate the runtime with the engine and expose game data.

The arrangement reduces low-level layout work and can accelerate revision. It also introduces licensing, integration, performance, and scripting boundaries that the engine must manage explicitly.

11608.sourceSearchName: game ui middleware game ui middleware
11608.title: Game UI Middleware
11608.heading: References

11609.sourceSearchName: game ui coordinate conversion game ui coordinate conversion
11609.title: Game UI Coordinate Conversion
11609.heading: Document

11610.sourceSearchName: game ui coordinate conversion game ui coordinate conversion
11610.title: Game UI Coordinate Conversion
11610.heading: Game UI Coordinate Conversion
11610.content:
Game UI coordinate conversion maps positions between a reference interface layout and the actual screen resolution. Scaling and offset rules preserve intended placement across displays with different dimensions and aspect ratios.

The conversion should distinguish absolute pixel artwork from elements that anchor to edges, centers, or safe regions. Pointer input must use the inverse mapping so visual and interactive bounds continue to agree.

11611.sourceSearchName: game ui coordinate conversion game ui coordinate conversion
11611.title: Game UI Coordinate Conversion
11611.heading: References

11612.sourceSearchName: game ui button state game ui button state
11612.title: Game UI Button State
11612.heading: Document

11613.sourceSearchName: game ui button state game ui button state
11613.title: Game UI Button State
11613.heading: Game UI Button State
11613.content:
A game UI button state records whether a button is normal, highlighted, pressed, or disabled. Input and focus transitions change the state, and each state can select different visual and audio feedback.

The button's activation event should remain separate from its appearance. This lets keyboard, gamepad, pointer, or touch navigation drive the same command while preserving appropriate feedback for the current interaction.

11614.sourceSearchName: game ui button state game ui button state
11614.title: Game UI Button State
11614.heading: References

11616.title: Game Tree
11616.heading: Game Tree
11616.content:
A game tree represents possible future states of an adversarial turn-based game. Each edge is a legal move, each level alternates the player to act, and terminal leaves record wins, losses, draws, or scores.

Complete trees grow too rapidly for most interesting games, so search stops at a depth limit and applies a [[Static Evaluation Function]]. [[Minimax]] then propagates estimated values back toward the current decision.

11618.sourceSearchName: game transformation matrix game transformation matrix
11618.title: Game Transformation Matrix
11618.heading: Document

11619.sourceSearchName: game transformation matrix game transformation matrix
11619.title: Game Transformation Matrix
11619.heading: Game Transformation Matrix
11619.content:
A game transformation matrix encodes a spatial operation such as scale, rotation, or translation in a form that can be applied consistently to points and directions. Homogeneous coordinates let translation participate in the same matrix machinery as linear transformations.

Combining transformations creates the matrices used to move geometry among model, world, camera, and projection spaces. The order matters because matrix multiplication is not commutative.

11620.title: Game Transformation Matrix

11621.heading: Document
11621.content:

Tags: [[Game Mechanics and Rules]] [[Play Design Elements]]

11622.title: Game Token
11622.heading: Game Token
11622.content:
A game token is a representational object with defined state and behavior. Tokens are the game's nouns: characters, cards, currency, territory, time, or any other object whose condition can be represented and changed.

Tokens communicate selected aspects of the [[Game Model]] to the player. Combined with [[Game Rule|rules]], they form [[Game Mechanic|mechanics]] and the concrete parts from which game systems are built.

11624.sourceSearchName: game time factor game time factor
11624.title: Game Time Factor
11624.heading: Document
11624.content:
2026-09-18 17:13

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Loop and Object Architecture]]

11625.sourceSearchName: game time factor game time factor
11625.title: Game Time Factor
11625.heading: Game Time Factor
11625.content:
A game time factor scales [[Real Delta Time]] before it advances the simulated world. A factor of one makes game time match real time, zero pauses simulation, and other values create slow motion or accelerated play.

The factor changes the time received by game-world updates without requiring the main [[Game Loop]] to stop. Interface animation or other systems that must continue during a pause can remain tied to real time instead.

11626.sourceSearchName: game time factor game time factor
11626.title: Game Time Factor
11626.heading: References

11627.title: Game Theme
11627.heading: Document
11627.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Authored Game Narrative]] [[Play Design Elements]]

11628.title: Game Theme
11628.heading: Game Theme
11628.content:
Game theme is what the player-facing experience means or is about. It is the outward expression of the game's underlying architecture, conveyed through fiction, art, sound, tokens, rules, and interaction.

Theme is strongest when each system and token derives meaning from it and supports the same whole. Elements that contradict the theme should be changed or removed rather than treated as disconnected decoration.

Images, animation, words, sound, and timing give rules a [[Game Context|context]] through which theme can be understood. When that context and the underlying mechanics behave coherently, the theme helps players form reliable expectations as well as interpretive meaning.

11630.sourceSearchName: game technology prototype game technology prototype
11630.title: Game Technology Prototype
11630.heading: Document

11631.sourceSearchName: game technology prototype game technology prototype
11631.title: Game Technology Prototype
11631.heading: Game Technology Prototype
11631.content:
A game technology prototype tests whether a platform, performance target, input device, rendering method, or asset pipeline can support the proposed design. It isolates technical uncertainty before the feature becomes entangled with production code and content.

The result may be a feasibility limit rather than a player-facing artifact. That limit still changes the design by revealing which experiences are affordable, reliable, or impossible under current constraints.

11632.sourceSearchName: game technology prototype game technology prototype
11632.title: Game Technology Prototype
11632.heading: References

11633.sourceSearchName: game team role clarity game team role clarity
11633.title: Game Team Role Clarity
11633.heading: Document

11634.sourceSearchName: game team role clarity game team role clarity
11634.title: Game Team Role Clarity
11634.heading: Game Team Role Clarity
11634.content:
Game-team role clarity makes visible who owns each responsibility, who contributes expertise, and who makes a final decision. It reduces duplicated effort and prevents essential work from being assumed to belong to someone else.

Roles describe accountability rather than rigid creative borders. Designers, programmers, artists, writers, and audio specialists still collaborate because a change in one discipline alters the player's combined experience.

11635.sourceSearchName: game team role clarity game team role clarity
11635.title: Game Team Role Clarity
11635.heading: References

11636.title: Game System
11636.heading: Document
11636.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Mechanics and Rules]] [[Game Systems]]

11637.title: Game System
11637.heading: Game System
11637.content:
A game system is a functional assembly of parts whose looping interactions perform a recognizable purpose within a game. Combat, progression, inventory, and crafting can each be treated as machines that produce particular forms of gameplay.

The parts and behaviors of a game system must support the desired player experience and connect coherently to peer and higher-level systems. A [[Game System Design Document]] records that purpose, structure, interactions, and context.

11639.sourceSearchName: game system design document game system design document
11639.title: Game System Design Document
11639.heading: Document

11640.sourceSearchName: game system design document game system design document
11640.title: Game System Design Document
11640.heading: Game System Design Document
11640.content:
A game system design document explains one system's name, purpose, desired player experience, looping structure, player interactions, and relationships to subsystems and peer systems. Diagrams make the important parts and behaviors visible.

Each system should have a brief separate document linked to the rest of the design rather than being buried in a monolithic bible. The document is living evidence of why the [[Game System]] has its current structure and must be updated as the design changes.

11641.sourceSearchName: game system design document game system design document
11641.title: Game System Design Document
11641.heading: References

11642.sourceSearchName: game team agreement game team agreement
11642.title: Game Team Agreement
11642.heading: Document

11643.sourceSearchName: game team agreement game team agreement
11643.title: Game Team Agreement
11643.heading: Game Team Agreement
11643.content:
A game team agreement records how collaborators will communicate, make decisions, handle credit, share files, meet deadlines, resolve conflict, and respond when commitments cannot be met. The team creates it together before pressure makes those expectations implicit.

The agreement is revisable evidence of consent, not a punishment mechanism. Revisiting it gives the group a neutral reference when working habits begin to harm trust or the project.

11644.sourceSearchName: game team agreement game team agreement
11644.title: Game Team Agreement
11644.heading: References

11645.title: Game Structure
11645.heading: Document
11645.content:
2026-09-18 16:43

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Design Process and Roles]]

11646.title: Game Structure
11646.heading: Game Structure
11646.content:
Game structure is the set of relationships among gameplay modes and the rules that move the game from one mode to another. It explains when different challenges, actions, views, and controls become available.

Shell menus sit outside active gameplay but still participate in the player's route through the software. A [[Flowboard]] makes the modes and transitions visible so omissions and confusing loops can be found before implementation.

11648.sourceSearchName: game state snapshot game state snapshot
11648.title: Game State Snapshot
11648.heading: Document

11649.sourceSearchName: game state snapshot game state snapshot
11649.title: Game State Snapshot
11649.heading: Game State Snapshot
11649.content:
A game state is a snapshot of every element that currently matters to play: object positions and properties, available actions, resource values, player progress, and the status of goals. An action changes some part of this state and thereby creates the situation for the next decision.

State is not the same as the full history of play. Two sessions can arrive at an identical visible state through different paths, although a game may preserve past events as state when they affect future possibilities.

11650.sourceSearchName: game state snapshot game state snapshot
11650.title: Game State Snapshot
11650.heading: References

11652.title: Game Sound
11652.heading: Game Sound
11652.content:
Game sound communicates through a channel that does not require the player to look away from current action. Distinct effects can identify objects, signal a state change, confirm success or failure, and indicate where an unseen threat has appeared.

Audio may reinforce visual information, clarify an ambiguous interaction, or deliberately oppose what is shown. Changes in pitch, loudness, rhythm, and timbre can also represent progress and influence player choice.

11654.sourceSearchName: game sound cue game sound cue
11654.title: Game Sound Cue
11654.heading: Document

11655.sourceSearchName: game sound cue game sound cue
11655.title: Game Sound Cue
11655.heading: Game Sound Cue
11655.content:
A game sound cue is a playback definition that associates one logical sound event with audio assets and metadata. The cue can specify variation, volume, looping, pitch, priority, and other rules instead of forcing gameplay code to manipulate files directly.

This layer separates the request to play a sound from the authored details of how it should be heard. Content can therefore change without rewriting the gameplay event that triggers it.

11656.sourceSearchName: game sound cue game sound cue
11656.title: Game Sound Cue
11656.heading: References

11658.title: Game Score
11658.heading: Game Score
11658.content:
A game score is an evaluation of selected player actions or outcomes. It converts aspects of a performance into numbers, grades, or categories that can be compared across attempts or between players.

Scoring communicates what the designer considers significant, but it is not inherently a [[Reward]] or [[Punishment]]. Players may pursue, reinterpret, or ignore the evaluation, especially in single-player games where no shared competition gives it authority.

11661.title: Game Scene
11661.heading: Game Scene
11661.content:
A game scene is the smallest useful unit of [[Game Pacing|pacing]] in which a distinct development of rules or play occurs. Depending on the game, a scene may be called a level, stage, round, wave, board, mission, or screen, but those labels do not determine its actual boundaries.

A scene arranges [[Game Verb|verbs]] and [[Game Part|objects]] so the player can encounter, understand, and apply particular relationships. One conventional level may contain several scenes when its focus or choice structure changes.

11663.title: Game Scope
11663.heading: Document
11663.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Production Planning and Milestones]]

11664.title: Game Scope
11664.heading: Game Scope
11664.content:
Game scope is the total amount of people, skills, time, systems, features, and content required to realize a design. It connects the desired experience to the practical cost and risk of creating it.

Scope is controlled through clear priorities and willingness to remove elements that do not support the [[Game Concept]]. Unreviewed additions create [[Scope Creep]], while a scope that omits core systems cannot deliver the intended experience.

11666.title: Game Rule
11666.heading: Document
11666.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Mechanics and Rules]] · [[Game Definition and Forms]] [[Play Design Elements]]

11667.title: Game Rule
11667.heading: Game Rule
11667.content:
A game rule specifies allowable behavior or a transition between states. Some rules are [[Game Verb|verbs]] that let the player act, while others determine how tokens behave, how resources change, and how objects respond.

Too few rules can leave important situations ambiguous, while too many rules and exceptions restrict agency and increase [[Cognitive Load]]. Consistent rules support [[Systemic Elegance]] and help players build a reliable [[Player Mental Model]].

The experience of play comes from rules interacting rather than operating in isolation. Rules become more useful as the player discovers their relationships and applies them in increasingly developed situations.

A complete ruleset may specify required, permitted, and prohibited actions; sequence of play; challenges and actions; goals; termination conditions; the meanings of symbols; and metarules that govern whether another rule may change. Software can hide bookkeeping rules from a video-game player while still enforcing them precisely.

11669.title: Game Resistance
11669.heading: Document
11669.content:
2026-09-05 15:28

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Challenge Design]] [[Play Design Elements]]

11670.title: Game Resistance
11670.heading: Game Resistance
11670.content:
Game resistance is the push and pull between a player's actions and the system's response. The player pushes through [[Game Verb|verbs]] and choices; the game pushes back through rules, obstacles, consequences, and limits, or pulls forward through goals and rewards.

Resistance includes more than difficulty. It also includes how widely the game opens its choices, how firmly rules refuse an action, how the experience changes over time, and whether the player can influence the pace or purpose of play.

11672.title: Game Release
11672.heading: Document
11672.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Production Planning and Milestones]]

11673.title: Game Release
11673.heading: Game Release
11673.content:
Game release is the transition from controlled development to availability for the intended public. It requires accepting that a creative work can be finished enough to deliver without becoming perfect in its creators' eyes.

Release also opens the outermost [[Designer Loop]]: broad player behavior and market response reveal lessons unavailable from prototypes or small playtests. Those lessons can guide later refinement, but the game must first become a real, accessible whole.

11675.sourceSearchName: game radar display game radar display
11675.title: Game Radar Display
11675.heading: Document

11676.sourceSearchName: game radar display game radar display
11676.title: Game Radar Display
11676.heading: Game Radar Display
11676.content:
A game radar display maps nearby world entities into a compact two-dimensional HUD region centered on or oriented around the player. Relative world positions are transformed, scaled, and clipped to the radar bounds.

The display may rotate with the player or preserve a fixed world orientation. Symbols compress spatial information, so filtering and prioritization are necessary when many entities occupy the same area.

11677.sourceSearchName: game radar display game radar display
11677.title: Game Radar Display
11677.heading: References

11678.sourceSearchName: game property saving hook game property saving hook
11678.title: Game Property Saving Hook
11678.heading: Document
11678.content:
2026-09-20 23:34

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Asset and Level Serialization]]

11679.sourceSearchName: game property saving hook game property saving hook
11679.title: Game Property Saving Hook
11679.heading: Game Property Saving Hook
11679.content:
A game property saving hook is a virtual operation that writes an actor's or component's type-specific state into a level record. Base implementations emit shared properties before derived implementations add their own fields.

Using a hook mirrors [[Game Property Loading Hook|loading]] and keeps the world serializer independent from concrete classes. Only durable authoring state should be written; runtime caches and temporary values can be reconstructed.

11680.sourceSearchName: game property saving hook game property saving hook
11680.title: Game Property Saving Hook
11680.heading: References

11681.sourceSearchName: game property loading hook game property loading hook
11681.title: Game Property Loading Hook
11681.heading: Document
11681.content:
2026-09-20 23:34

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Asset and Level Serialization]]

11682.sourceSearchName: game property loading hook game property loading hook
11682.title: Game Property Loading Hook
11682.heading: Game Property Loading Hook
11682.content:
A game property loading hook is a virtual operation through which an actor or component reads its type-specific fields from parsed level data. Base implementations load common properties, and derived implementations extend that behavior.

The hook separates object construction from configuration and keeps the central loader from depending on every concrete field. Missing optional values can retain defaults, while required values should be validated explicitly.

11683.sourceSearchName: game property loading hook game property loading hook
11683.title: Game Property Loading Hook
11683.heading: References

11684.title: Game Process
11684.heading: Document
11684.content:
2026-09-18 16:43

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Core Mechanics and Internal Economies]]

11685.title: Game Process
11685.heading: Game Process
11685.content:
A game process is a mechanic that operates over time rather than completing at one instant. Movement, production, regeneration, decay, and a spreading environmental effect are processes.

A process needs a start condition, update rule, timing model, and stopping condition. Its rates and dependencies often determine the behavior of an internal economy.

11687.title: Game Pitch
11687.heading: Document
11687.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Production Planning and Milestones]]

11688.title: Game Pitch
11688.heading: Game Pitch
11688.content:
A game pitch communicates a game's vision persuasively to obtain a particular response, such as funding, validation, coverage, or team participation. Its content and depth change with the audience, context, and requested outcome.

An effective pitch opens with a concise [[Concept Statement]], shows the core experience with appropriate evidence, and limits detail to what the audience needs to build confidence. It ends with a clear call to action and is refined through practice and feedback.

11690.title: Game Part
11690.heading: Document
11690.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Systems]] [[Game Mechanics and Rules]]

11691.title: Game Part
11691.heading: Game Part
11691.content:
A game part is a physical, conceptual, or representational element with internal state and behaviors. At the atomic level it is specified through [[Game Attribute|attributes]], values, and functions rather than through smaller systemic loops.

Parts are the nouns and verbs from which loops arise: attributes hold state, while behaviors change resources and connect parts. Each included part should support player interaction, a system purpose, or the internal model needed for the experience.

From the player's perspective, a part can function as the object of a [[Game Verb]]: the thing acted on that completes an interactive relationship. Useful objects reinforce important verbs and interact with other objects instead of existing for one isolated case.

11693.title: Game Pacing
11693.heading: Document
11693.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Balance and Progression]] [[Level and Scene Design]] [[Game Challenge Design]] [[Level Layout and Progression]]

11694.title: Game Pacing
11694.heading: Game Pacing
11694.content:
Game pacing is the rate and rhythm at which activity, challenge, reward, and progression unfold. It can be measured through actions, completed challenges, attention, or elapsed time rather than through levels alone.

Pacing balances early success with lasting goals and alternates intensity to avoid fatigue. [[Progression Curve|Progression curves]] set the broad rate, while nested interaction loops and playtests reveal how that rate feels to the player.

Within a [[Game Scene]], pacing can emerge as the [[Scene Shape|shape of choice]] widens and narrows. Ordering scenes determines when rules are introduced, revisited, combined, or inverted, so rhythm can change without continually adding new mechanics.

Within a level, layout, enemy placement, resources, traversal time, story events, and safe areas determine the rate of demand and recovery. Varying that rate keeps sustained intensity from becoming exhausting and keeps quiet stretches from becoming monotonous.

11696.title: Game Object
11696.heading: Document
11696.content:
2026-09-18 17:13

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Loop and Object Architecture]]

11697.title: Game Object
11697.heading: Game Object
11697.content:
A game object is a program-level representation of something that participates in the running game world. Different objects may need to update over time, draw visual output, do both, or provide other specialized behavior.

Separating capabilities into interfaces such as [[Updateable Game Object]] and [[Drawable Game Object]] avoids requiring every object to perform every phase. The world can then keep registries organized by behavior rather than by a single rigid class hierarchy.

11699.sourceSearchName: game network socket game network socket
11699.title: Game Network Socket
11699.heading: Document

11700.sourceSearchName: game network socket game network socket
11700.title: Game Network Socket
11700.heading: Game Network Socket
11700.content:
A game network socket is the operating-system interface through which a game sends and receives transport data. It is created for a protocol family and transport type, then bound, connected, listened on, or addressed according to the chosen topology.

Stream sockets commonly expose [[Transmission Control Protocol]], while datagram sockets expose [[User Datagram Protocol]]. The game layer still owns message framing, serialization, validation, and integration with the update loop.

11701.sourceSearchName: game network socket game network socket
11701.title: Game Network Socket
11701.heading: References

11702.sourceSearchName: game network cheat prevention game network cheat prevention
11702.title: Game Network Cheat Prevention
11702.heading: Document

11703.sourceSearchName: game network cheat prevention game network cheat prevention
11703.title: Game Network Cheat Prevention
11703.heading: Game Network Cheat Prevention
11703.content:
Game network cheat prevention minimizes how much authority and hidden information an untrusted client receives. A server can validate movement, combat, inventory, and timing claims instead of accepting client state at face value.

Defenses also include protected transport, code and memory checks, anomaly detection, and limiting packet information to what the player should know. No single countermeasure removes cheating, so topology and protocol design must reduce exploitable trust from the start.

11704.sourceSearchName: game network cheat prevention game network cheat prevention
11704.title: Game Network Cheat Prevention
11704.heading: References

11705.title: Game Narrative
11705.heading: Document
11705.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Authored Game Narrative]] [[Emergent Game Narrative]]

11706.title: Game Narrative
11706.heading: Game Narrative
11706.content:
Game narrative is a connected sequence of events made meaningful to the people involved. It can be authored directly, arise from play, or combine a fictional premise with systemic events chosen by the player.

Highly prescribed narrative narrows the [[Play Space]], while a premise can scaffold interpretation without fixing one path. Systemic narrative gains authenticity from player agency but gives the designer less precise control over the resulting story.

An [[Authored Story]] is deliberately carried by the game, while an [[Emergent Story]] is the account produced through a particular act of playing. Games can combine both, letting authored context and systemic events inform how the player interprets the experience.

11708.title: Game Model
11708.heading: Document
11708.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Mechanics and Rules]] [[Game Systems]]

11709.title: Game Model
11709.heading: Game Model
11709.content:
A game model is the game's simplified, dynamic representation of a world. It includes the combined parts, states, rules, and systems that respond to player actions and create the space for gameplay.

The model does not need to reproduce reality in full; it must expose the structure relevant to the experience. Consistent [[Feedback]] allows the player's [[Player Mental Model|mental model]] to track it closely enough for prediction and meaningful action.

11711.sourceSearchName: game menu system game menu system
11711.title: Game Menu System
11711.heading: Document

11712.sourceSearchName: game menu system game menu system
11712.title: Game Menu System
11712.heading: Game Menu System
11712.content:
A game menu system presents interactive screens for actions such as starting play, changing settings, pausing, or managing saved data. Each screen owns visible elements and maps player input to navigation or commands.

The system must coordinate focus, selection, transitions, and return behavior across many screens. A [[Game Menu State Machine]] or [[Game Menu Stack]] makes those relationships explicit instead of scattering menu rules through individual buttons.

11713.sourceSearchName: game menu system game menu system
11713.title: Game Menu System
11713.heading: References

11715.title: Game Modding
11715.heading: Game Modding
11715.content:
Game modding is the alteration or extension of a game by players using exposed code, data, or creation tools. Mods can add characters, quests, scenarios, objects, rules, or entirely new experiences to an existing system and world.

Modding is a form of [[Shared Authorship]] that can keep a game evolving beyond its original content. Supporting it may require substantial tool design, documentation, and examples that help players understand how to create coherent additions.

11717.sourceSearchName: game menu state machine game menu state machine
11717.title: Game Menu State Machine
11717.heading: Document

11718.sourceSearchName: game menu state machine game menu state machine
11718.title: Game Menu State Machine
11718.heading: Game Menu State Machine
11718.content:
A game menu state machine represents each menu screen as a state and navigation actions as transitions. Only the active state receives input and determines which interface elements are updated and drawn.

This model makes legal transitions explicit and works well when navigation has a controlled structure. A [[Game Menu Stack]] is useful when screens frequently overlay one another and need automatic return to the previous screen.

11719.sourceSearchName: game menu state machine game menu state machine
11719.title: Game Menu State Machine
11719.heading: References

11720.sourceSearchName: game menu stack game menu stack
11720.title: Game Menu Stack
11720.heading: Document

11721.sourceSearchName: game menu stack game menu stack
11721.title: Game Menu Stack
11721.heading: Game Menu Stack
11721.content:
A game menu stack stores interface screens in navigation order. Pushing a screen places it above the current one, while popping it reveals the previous screen without requiring every overlay to know its caller.

Pause dialogs and nested option screens fit this structure naturally. The system must define whether covered screens continue updating or drawing and how input is restricted to the topmost active layer.

11722.sourceSearchName: game menu stack game menu stack
11722.title: Game Menu Stack
11722.heading: References

11724.title: Game Mechanic
11724.heading: Game Mechanic
11724.content:
A game mechanic is an identifiable interactive loop formed from [[Game Token|tokens]], [[Game Rule|rules]], the player, and the game. It may be brief, such as drawing a card, or contain many subsystems and take much longer, such as building an empire.

Mechanics can recur across otherwise different games because their loop structure is separable from a particular theme. Repeated central mechanics become [[Core Gameplay Loop|core gameplay]] and often help define a [[Game Genre]].

A mechanic becomes legible through a vocabulary of [[Game Verb|player verbs]], objects, and their relationships. Its quality depends less on the number of available actions than on how strongly those actions create choices and reinforce one another.

11727.title: Game Lore
11727.heading: Game Lore
11727.content:
Game lore is optional story material that fills in the background of a game's world, characters, and history. It commonly appears through readable objects, conversations, artifacts, and environmental details discovered during exploration.

Lore supports the main narrative by adding flavor and context rather than necessarily advancing the plot. If understanding it becomes essential to the central story, treating it as entirely optional can make important meaning easy to miss.

11729.title: Game Loop
11729.heading: Document
11729.content:
2026-09-18 17:13

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Loop and Object Architecture]]

11730.title: Game Loop
11730.heading: Game Loop
11730.content:
A game loop is the repeating control structure that keeps a game running. Each pass processes input, updates the game world, and generates outputs such as graphics and sound before beginning the next [[Game Frame]].

The order is deliberate: input changes intentions, the update phase advances state, and output presents the resulting state. Timing and object registries turn this simple cycle into a coordinated real-time architecture.

11733.title: Game Localization
11733.heading: Game Localization
11733.content:
Game localization adapts content for sale in another country or cultural market. It includes language and idiom as well as symbols, humor, laws, ratings, controls, payment expectations, and sensitivities about violence, sexuality, religion, or politics.

Literal translation is therefore insufficient. A localized game must remain understandable and acceptable without erasing the experience or introducing conflicts between altered presentation and unchanged mechanics.

Interface implementation must anticipate that translated text changes length and may require different glyphs or layout. Localization can also require region-specific art or content changes when laws prohibit particular symbols or depictions.

11735.sourceSearchName: game level saving game level saving
11735.title: Game Level Saving
11735.heading: Document
11735.content:
2026-09-20 23:34

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Asset and Level Serialization]]

11736.sourceSearchName: game level saving game level saving
11736.title: Game Level Saving
11736.heading: Game Level Saving
11736.content:
Game level saving walks the current world and writes global settings followed by each persistent actor, its type, properties, and components. Virtual saving hooks let derived runtime types contribute fields without central code knowing every property.

Transient actors and components may be excluded so temporary effects do not become authored content. The output must conform to the same [[Level File Schema]] expected by [[Game Level Loading]].

11737.sourceSearchName: game level saving game level saving
11737.title: Game Level Saving
11737.heading: References

11738.sourceSearchName: game level loading game level loading
11738.title: Game Level Loading
11738.heading: Document
11738.content:
2026-09-20 23:34

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Asset and Level Serialization]]

11739.sourceSearchName: game level loading game level loading
11739.title: Game Level Loading
11739.heading: Game Level Loading
11739.content:
Game level loading parses a [[Level File Schema]], applies global properties, constructs actors by type, attaches their components, and assigns saved properties. Construction and property assignment are separate so the correct runtime type exists before specialized values are read.

The loader must handle missing or malformed fields without leaving a partially registered world. Type dispatch and property hooks keep file parsing independent from individual actor classes.

11740.sourceSearchName: game level loading game level loading
11740.title: Game Level Loading
11740.heading: References

11741.sourceSearchName: game interface prototype game interface prototype
11741.title: Game Interface Prototype
11741.heading: Document

11742.sourceSearchName: game interface prototype game interface prototype
11742.title: Game Interface Prototype
11742.heading: Game Interface Prototype
11742.content:
A game interface prototype explores how players issue commands and receive information or feedback. It may test screen layout, navigation, controller mapping, gesture, physical input, or the transition between interface states.

Its fidelity should match the uncertainty. Clickable wireframes can answer flow questions, while timing and embodied control may require a working input device and a responsive scene.

11743.sourceSearchName: game interface prototype game interface prototype
11743.title: Game Interface Prototype
11743.heading: References

11744.sourceSearchName: game interface accessibility game interface accessibility
11744.title: Game Interface Accessibility
11744.heading: Document

11745.sourceSearchName: game interface accessibility game interface accessibility
11745.title: Game Interface Accessibility
11745.heading: Game Interface Accessibility
11745.content:
Game interface accessibility designs controls and presentation so people with differing visual, auditory, motor, or other abilities can perceive information and perform required actions. It includes more than adding an easy mode.

Color should not be the sole carrier of state, spoken dialogue can be subtitled, critical audio can have visual equivalents, and control demands can be adjustable. Accessibility works best when included in the interface architecture rather than patched onto finished content.

11746.sourceSearchName: game interface accessibility game interface accessibility
11746.title: Game Interface Accessibility
11746.heading: References

11747.sourceSearchName: game interaction model game interaction model
11747.title: Game Interaction Model
11747.heading: Document

11748.sourceSearchName: game interaction model game interaction model
11748.title: Game Interaction Model
11748.heading: Game Interaction Model
11748.content:
A game interaction model defines how the player projects intention into the game world. It identifies the entities the player controls, the scope of that control, and the operations the interface must make available.

The interaction model is one component of a [[Gameplay Mode]], alongside gameplay and camera model. Avatar-based, party-based, multipresent, contestant, and desktop models create different requirements for selection, navigation, and feedback.

11749.sourceSearchName: game interaction model game interaction model
11749.title: Game Interaction Model
11749.heading: References

11751.title: Game Hook
11751.heading: Game Hook
11751.content:
A game hook is a call to action that combines a perceivable opportunity with enough motivation for the player to act. It gives the player a reason to enter or continue an interactive loop.

An effective hook supports an understandable early goal and timely positive [[Feedback]], allowing the player to begin a [[Player Mental Model]]. It must lead into the real [[Core Gameplay Loop]] rather than substitute spectacle for the game's enduring activity.

11754.title: Game Idea
11754.heading: Game Idea
11754.content:
A game idea is an initial possibility for an activity, situation, mechanic, fantasy, or experience that might become a game. Ideas can come from dreams of doing, other media, observed systems, existing games, or unexpected parts of ordinary life.

An idea is not yet a [[Game Concept]]. It becomes actionable only after the designer explains what the player does, who the game serves, how it progresses, and why its structure can produce the intended experience.

11757.title: Game Handicap
11757.heading: Game Handicap
11757.content:
A game handicap adjusts rules or victory conditions to compensate for differences in player skill. It gives a less experienced participant a credible chance without requiring both players to face an identical task.

A handicap should preserve agency and be understandable to everyone involved. It balances participants, whereas a difficulty mode ordinarily changes the player's relationship to the environment.

11759.title: Game Goal
11759.heading: Document
11759.content:
2026-09-18 16:43

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Definition and Forms]] [[Play Design Elements]]

11760.title: Game Goal
11760.heading: Game Goal
11760.content:
A game goal is a desired result or condition that a player works toward. A game may contain many nested goals, and a goal can organize activity even when it is difficult or impossible to complete.

Goals must be nontrivial enough to require meaningful effort. Victory and loss conditions are special goal-related rules, but open-ended play can remain game-like without a final victory condition when players still pursue intermediate goals.

11762.title: Game Genre
11762.heading: Document
11762.content:
2026-09-05 14:36

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Design Methods]] · [[Video Game Genres and Platforms]]

11763.title: Game Genre
11763.heading: Game Genre
11763.content:
A game genre is a heuristic label for a familiar cluster of dominant gameplay and interaction conventions. It lets designers and players quickly anticipate likely mechanics and experiences.

Because the label compresses many distinct qualities, it can encourage lazy design or hide important differences. Describing specific [[Game Mechanic|mechanics]], timescales, and player activities gives a more precise account than relying on genre alone.

The source defines genre chiefly through characteristic kinds of challenges, regardless of setting or visual content. A familiar genre lowers communication and design risk by supplying expected actions, while a hybrid deliberately combines challenge patterns from more than one genre.

11765.sourceSearchName: game genre hybridization game genre hybridization
11765.title: Game Genre Hybridization
11765.heading: Document

11766.sourceSearchName: game genre hybridization game genre hybridization
11766.title: Game Genre Hybridization
11766.heading: Game Genre Hybridization
11766.content:
Game genre hybridization combines substantial challenge and action patterns from more than one established genre. A hybrid can create a distinctive experience when the parts serve a common player role and premise.

Combining genres increases design and development work and does not automatically combine their audiences. The mixture should be playtested early because players attracted to one pattern may dislike the other.

11767.sourceSearchName: game genre hybridization game genre hybridization
11767.title: Game Genre Hybridization
11767.heading: References

11768.title: Game Frame
11768.heading: Document
11768.content:
2026-09-18 17:13

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Loop and Object Architecture]]

11769.title: Game Frame
11769.heading: Game Frame
11769.content:
A game frame is one complete iteration of the [[Game Loop]], including input processing, world updates, and output generation. The amount of real time between consecutive frames is the [[Real Delta Time]].

Rendering speed determines how often frames are presented, but simulation behavior should not silently depend on that frequency. Frame-based work therefore uses elapsed time when computing motion and other continuous change.

11771.sourceSearchName: game feedback element game feedback element
11771.title: Game Feedback Element
11771.heading: Document

11772.sourceSearchName: game feedback element game feedback element
11772.title: Game Feedback Element
11772.heading: Game Feedback Element
11772.content:
A game feedback element is a visible or audible interface component that tells the player the effect of an action or supplies state needed for the next decision. Animation, sound, indicators, text, and controller response can all serve this role.

Good feedback is timely and attributable: the player can connect the signal to the action or event that caused it. Redundant sensory channels can improve clarity and accessibility.

11773.sourceSearchName: game feedback element game feedback element
11773.title: Game Feedback Element
11773.heading: References

11774.title: Game Event
11774.heading: Document
11774.content:
2026-09-18 16:43

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Core Mechanics and Internal Economies]]

11775.title: Game Event
11775.heading: Game Event
11775.content:
A game event is a discrete occurrence that changes state at a particular moment. A player action, collision, purchase, trigger, or timer completion can generate an event.

Events connect conditions to consequences. Their design should state when they occur, what information they carry, and which entities or processes respond.
